title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 114 (Ordinary and special resolutions)

content.overview: A resolution shall be an ordinary resolution if the notice required under this Act has been duly given and it is required to be passed by the votes cast, whether on a show of hands, or electronically or on a poll, as the case may be, in favour of the resolution, including the casting vote, if any, of the Chairman, by members who, being entitled so to do, vote in person, or where proxies are allowed, by proxy or by postal ballot, exceed the votes, if any, cast against the resolution by members so entitled and voting. A resolution shall be a special resolution when the intention to propose the resolution as a special resolution has been duly specified in the notice or other intimation, the notice required under this Act has been duly given, and the votes cast in favour are not less than three times the number of votes, if any, cast against the resolution.
content.glance: Ordinary: votes in favour exceed votes against among members entitled to vote and voting, after due notice. Special: notice must specify the intention, and votes in favour must be not less than three times votes against.
content.study:
## Section 114 — Ordinary and special resolutions

**Ordinary resolution (subsection (1)).** The notice required under the Act must be duly given, and the votes cast in favour (including the Chairman's casting vote, if any) by members entitled to vote and voting must exceed the votes cast against.

**Special resolution (subsection (2)).** The intention to propose the resolution as a special resolution must be duly specified in the notice or other intimation; the notice required under the Act must be duly given; and the votes cast in favour must be not less than three times the number of votes, if any, cast against.

## Apply the provision
- Identify whether the resolution is ordinary or special under the enabling provision.
- Check notice compliance and, for a special resolution, the intention statement.
- Compare votes cast for and against among members entitled to vote and voting — not the total membership on the register.

This note is a focused study aid; the topic remains under source and current-law review.

provisions.title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 114 (Ordinary and special resolutions)

examples.title: Ordinary threshold only
examples.body: 100 votes for and 40 against meets the ordinary voting test but not the special-resolution ratio. Educational illustration only.

examples.title: Special-resolution ratio
examples.body: 120 votes for and 40 against meets the 3:1 ratio if notice requirements are also satisfied. Educational illustration only.

hypotheticals.question: A resolution is proposed as special but the notice does not state that intention. Votes in favour are four times votes against. Is it a special resolution?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Subsection (2) requires that the intention to propose it as a special resolution is duly specified in the notice or other intimation. A numerical majority cannot cure a missing special-resolution notice statement.

misconceptions.trap: Calculating the majority from the total number of members on the register.
misconceptions.correction: The comparison is between votes cast for and against by members entitled to vote and voting.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming a strong vote cures a defective special-resolution notice.
misconceptions.correction: Notice of intention and the 3:1 voting test are cumulative.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What does section 114 provide?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: It distinguishes ordinary resolutions (simple majority of votes cast after due notice) from special resolutions (intention stated in notice, and votes in favour not less than three times votes against).
